messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 61-year-old bus driver who came to treatment after months of worsening nights, telling his wife he felt more on guard after dark than at any other time of day. Years earlier, he had been detained and tortured. When he first described it, the account came in jagged pieces rather than a smooth narrative: a concrete room, the smell of damp fabric, footsteps outside a door, a burst of pain, someone else crying out nearby. Some moments stood out with unbearable sharpness, while long stretches felt missing altogether. What stayed most alive in him was not only what was done to him, but his conviction that he had failed other people who were there. He had come to believe he should have stopped it, should have protected them, and that the fact he had not done so proved something basic and shameful about him—that he was weak.

Those beliefs shaped the way he remembered the trauma. When he tried to think about what happened, he did not arrive at a fuller story or any sense of perspective; instead he was pulled toward the same accusing conclusion. The fragments he could access most clearly were the ones that seemed to confirm his self-condemnation: hearing others, being unable to intervene, feeling overpowered. The blank spaces troubled him almost as much as the vivid images. He would say that if whole sections were missing, perhaps there had been some moment when he could have done more and had failed to. In that way, the gaps in memory became proof to him rather than uncertainty, feeding his sense that he had not protected others and would never forgive himself.

Remembering also brought back the original terror with startling force. A sound, a smell, even a certain quality of footsteps could seem to collapse time, and his body reacted before he had fully oriented himself. At home at night, if the house settled or he heard movement outside, he would feel a surge of alarm and listen intently for signs that someone was trying to enter. Because the original experience remained so broken—certain moments crystal clear, others blank—he never felt he had a settled past event behind him. Instead it was as if danger could still emerge from the missing pieces. The memory itself kept him scanning, especially in darkness, straining to catch the first sign of intrusion.

His work as a bus driver gave these reactions a daily setting. On late shifts, when passengers boarded heavily and the bus filled with the sound of boots on the steps or voices from the rear, he could feel his chest tighten and his hands go slick on the wheel. He knew he was on a city route in daylight, yet his body responded as though something was about to happen. By the time he got home, he was already wound tight, and once night fell he moved through the house checking locks and pausing at small noises. He listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering, and his wife had noticed that he rarely settled fully into bed. The hypervigilance was not experienced by him as excessive; it felt necessary, because he was certain that a man who had once failed to protect others could not afford to miss danger again.

That same vigilance deepened his shame. Each night of listening at doors and windows seemed to David like evidence that he had been permanently changed by what happened, and not in a way he could respect. He saw his fear as weakness. What frightened him almost as much as the noises themselves was what his reaction to them seemed to say about his character. He believed other men would have recovered, or would have fought harder then, or would not still be living this way now. The more alert and physically reactive he became, the more he judged himself, and those judgments made the nights feel even less safe.

Over time the loop tightened. The fragments of memory reignited terror; the terror kept him monitoring for threat; the monitoring was taken as proof that he was weak and had failed; and that harsh self-appraisal drew him back again to the worst, sharpest parts of the trauma. He did not describe broad symptoms beyond this so much as a narrowing of life around nighttime and vigilance. His wife urged him to get help after he admitted that evenings had become something he dreaded hours in advance, and that even in his own home he listened like a man waiting for a door to break open. What finally brought him in was not only exhaustion, but the fear that he would die still believing the same thing he told himself in session: that when it mattered most, he had failed others, and that the terror had never really ended.
